name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,408

clue.text: I love wearing rough pants up against it

indicators.note: a word wearing another has that other draped around it like clothing
something rough is roughed up or knocked about, so the letters that follow come out disordered

blocks.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to a liking for wearing scratchy underwear while backed up against something.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged pants become NASPT, and the O slips in between P and T to give IN A SPOT after the opening I.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a spot is an idiom for facing difficulty, just as being up against it means struggling with trouble.

clue.text: Hoskins is mature? That's something to picture

blocks.note: Hoskins is the setter, so the setter saying 'Hoskins is' says I'M
to mature is to age, as wine or cheese does

explanation.surface: The setter wonders aloud whether they have grown up, then offers something to imagine.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by their own pen name, standing for I or ME; here the name plus 'is' stands for I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a picture held in the mind or shown visually, a thing one can picture.

clue.text: One in local getting drunk with endless hock?

definitions.text: One in local getting drunk with endless hock?

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the word is cut off
a drunk staggers about out of order, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written
hock, a German white wine, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A regular at the pub gets plastered on German white wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a drinker at the local, sozzled on hock, is exactly the answer. Hock is a German white wine; a local is one's nearby pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone habitually getting plastered at the pub on wine fits a person addicted to drink.

clue.text: Bucket of drink brought up, I must tuck into it!

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing a word up means reading it from bottom to top
to tuck into something is to go inside it

blocks.note: to lap is to drink, as a cat does
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is handed a whole bucket of drink and resolves to tuck in.
explanation.walkthrough: LAP turned upwards is PAL, and the I goes into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pail is an open container with a handle for carrying liquid, the same thing as a bucket.

clue.text: Miserly guards working between 6 and 12?

indicators.note: a guard stands round what it protects, so one word surrounds the other

blocks.note: tight is informal for stingy with money
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: Stingy employers keep watch over staff on a shift that runs from six till twelve.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers look like a shift's hours or a score; read as clock times, six to midnight is the evening of today.
explanation.definitionFit: This evening, from six o'clock until midnight, is the span the word names when said during the day.

clue.text: My gas will hamper small booty-grabber!

indicators.note: to hamper is to hem in, so the following word is held inside

blocks.note: 'my!' and 'cor!' are both exclamations of surprise
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
air is a gas, or mixture of gases

explanation.surface: An exclamation about wind slowing down a little pirate.
explanation.walkthrough: Cor is a British exclamation of surprise, much like 'my!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A corsair was a Barbary pirate who seized ships and their plunder, so a grabber of booty.

clue.text: Item of luggage in taxi close to the Savoy?

indicators.note: one word sits in another, enclosed by it
the close of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: a cab is a taxi
a bag is a piece of luggage
the last letter of the

explanation.surface: A suitcase arrives by taxi near the Savoy, the famous London hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Savoy' reads as the London hotel, but 'the' only supplies its last letter and Savoy alone is the definition, a variety of crinkly-leaved vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Savoy is a variety of the green leafy vegetable with crinkled leaves, so an example signalled by the question mark.

clue.text: Truly awful that leader has left hollow legacy

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and it has gone
something hollow has had its insides taken out, leaving only the outside letters

blocks.note: awful is frightful, which loses its first letter
the first and last letters of legacy

explanation.surface: A grim tale of an inheritance gutted after the head of the family dies.
explanation.walkthrough: FRIGHTFUL minus its F gives RIGHTFUL, and LY is added to make RIGHTFULLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Rightfully means properly or justly, by right; the setter treats it as a loose equivalent of genuinely or in truth.

clue.text: Extraterrestrial area one like Armstrong climbs

indicators.note: in a down clue, a word that climbs is read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for area
Neil Armstrong, the first man on the moon, is one with the first name Neil

explanation.surface: A space visitor clambers about like an astronaut on the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: Neil Armstrong was the first man on the moon; 'one like Armstrong' is anyone sharing his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: An alien is a being from another planet, which is what extraterrestrial means as a noun.

clue.text: They fight against things concerning siblings

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a business letter
sisters are female siblings

explanation.surface: Brothers and sisters squabbling over possessions.
explanation.definitionFit: Resisters are people who oppose or stand firm against something, the ones who fight back.

clue.text: Where one can see lots of you in motion

indicators.note: one word goes in another, enclosed by it

blocks.note: action is motion or movement
U is text-speak for you

explanation.surface: A camera or mirror shows plenty of you moving about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots of you' reads as many images of you, but 'lots' ends the definition: items for sale at a sale by bidding.
explanation.definitionFit: Lots are the numbered items put up for bidding, and an auction is the sale where they are seen and sold.

clue.text: What egotistical bald men might put on heads?

definitions.text: What egotistical bald men might put on heads?

blocks.clueFragment: What egotistical bald men might put on heads?
blocks.note: surface reading: vain balding men choosing a hairpiece
setter's reading: heads are important people, and the answer names them as a whole

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer and it is large hairpieces, just what a vain bald man might wear; as one word it means people of importance.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigwigs are important people, the heads of organisations, so vanity hairpieces and top people share one phrase.

clue.text: Drug company importing heroin and E?

indicators.note: a company importing goods takes them inside

blocks.note: E is ecstasy
Co is the abbreviation for company
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A pharmaceutical firm brings in heroin and ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: The final E looks like another drug, but it is the definition: the letter E in the radio alphabet. CO takes in H after the E.
explanation.definitionFit: Echo is the code word for the letter E in the NATO phonetic alphabet used in radio.

clue.text: Genitals injured gathering New England roses

indicators.note: something injured is damaged and bent out of shape, so its letters are rearranged
to gather something is to take it in, enclosing it

blocks.note: taken as written
NE is the abbreviation for New England

explanation.surface: A painful accident involving thorny bushes in New England.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude-looking surface is a cover: the flowers are wild roses, also called sweetbriar.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is sweetbriar, a wild pink rose, so eglantines are a kind of rose.

clue.text: Wild ride in a man's Pontiac?

indicators.note: something wild is unruly and out of order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A man takes a thrilling drive in his Pontiac car.
explanation.walkthrough: Pontiac reads as the American car make, but it is the eighteenth-century Ottawa chief who led a rising against the British.
explanation.definitionFit: Pontiac was an Ottawa leader, one of the indigenous peoples of America, so an example of the term.

clue.text: Unit of distance? More like time, stupid!

indicators.note: something stupid makes no sense, so the letters are muddled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone scolds a person for measuring time with a unit of distance.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilometre is a metric measure of length, a thousand metres, so a unit of distance.

clue.text: Tease snoozer and he might take issue!

blocks.note: to kid is to tease or joke with
one who naps is a snoozer

explanation.surface: Wind up someone who is dozing and they will probably object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take issue' looks like disagreeing, but issue means offspring, so taking issue is snatching children.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue means children, and one who abducts a child is the criminal who takes it.

clue.text: After knocking it back, couple gets loose

indicators.note: knocking something back turns it round, so these two letters are read the other way

blocks.note: to couple is to join or unite

explanation.surface: After downing a drink, a pair of people loosen up.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the two letters of 'it' inside the word for couple are turned round, and the joining word becomes its own opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: To untie a knot is to undo it, which is to loose it in the old verb sense of set free.

clue.text: Sort of holiday home mates hire out

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Friends club together to rent a holiday property.
explanation.definitionFit: A timeshare is a property whose use is split among several owners, each having it for set weeks a year.

clue.text: Interior design staff reflected about city

indicators.note: a reflection shows things the wrong way round
a word placed about another goes round it

blocks.note: a rod is a staff or stick
EC is the postcode area for the City of London

explanation.surface: Office workers in the city mirror their surroundings in their furnishings.
explanation.walkthrough: EC is the London postal district covering the financial City.
explanation.definitionFit: Decor is the furnishing and decoration of a room, the result of interior design.

clue.text: Retired male sadly blocks toilets in US town

indicators.note: retiring is drawing back, so the following letters run backwards
whatever blocks a passage sits inside it

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for male
alas is said sadly, as a lament
loo is British slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: An old pensioner's sad plumbing mishap in an American town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' looks like a description of the male, but it reverses the next two pieces together. A loo is British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Los Alamos is the New Mexico town where the atomic bomb was developed, so a place in the US.

clue.text: Dish in sink being tackled by Lois?

indicators.note: a player being tackled is wrapped up by the tackler, so one word is held within another

blocks.note: Lois Lane is Superman's girlfriend, reporter on the Daily Planet
to sag is to sink or droop

explanation.surface: A plate left in the kitchen sink for someone called Lois to wash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish in sink' paints washing up, but 'in' is a link and sink is a verb. Lois stands for her surname, Lane, from the Superman stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagne is an Italian baked dish of pasta sheets layered with sauce, so a dish in the food sense.

clue.text: Drink all over spring and get fat fast

indicators.note: one word spread all over another covers it on every side

blocks.note: to sup is to drink
a well or spring is a source of water

explanation.surface: Drinking lots of spring water and piling on weight fast.
explanation.definitionFit: To swell up is to grow bigger or puff out quickly, as a swollen body becomes fat in a hurry.

clue.text: Direct a clergyman to inhale bit of dope

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a single letter of it, here the first
inhaling takes something inside

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of dope
a minister is a member of the clergy

explanation.surface: Instructions for getting a vicar to take a drag of cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: A MINISTER takes the D just after its opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: To administer is to manage or run affairs, so to direct them.

clue.text: Wettish opposition leader shrouded in fog ...

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
something shrouded is wrapped inside a covering

blocks.note: mist is thin fog
the first letter of opposition

explanation.surface: A political opposition leader lost in fog, dithering and wet.
explanation.walkthrough: The O goes inside MIST. The ellipsis links to the next clue for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: Moist means slightly wet or damp, which is what wettish describes.

clue.text: When Hoskins was essentially continent?

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so its middle letter is taken

blocks.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
Hoskins is the setter, who speaks of himself as I
the middle letter of was

explanation.surface: The setter reminisces about once being, at heart, continental.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often use their own pen name to mean I or ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is the largest of the Earth's continents, so a direct example of the category.

clue.text: ... helped a journalist to bring in papers

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside

blocks.note: taken as written
ED is short for editor, a newspaper journalist
ID means identity papers

explanation.surface: A reporter fetching newspapers to help out.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to the previous clue for the surface only; ED for editor is a crossword staple for a journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Aided means assisted or gave support to, the same as helped.

clue.text: Garden tools caught in stockings

blocks.note: first meaning: flexible pipes for watering, here used as a plural
second meaning: an old word for stockings and tights, as in hosiery

explanation.surface: Gardening implements tangled up in a pair of stockings.
explanation.walkthrough: Hose can stand for a collection of watering pipes as well as for legwear; 'caught in' just joins the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Watering pipes used in gardens and women's leg coverings both go by this one word, which serves as a plural.

clue.text: Old man having one round for twosome?

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man
one is the Roman numeral I
a ring is round, a circle

explanation.surface: Dad buying a single round of drinks for a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is British slang for one's father, giving PA.
explanation.definitionFit: A pairing is two people or things put together, which is what a twosome is.

clue.text: Horror writer about to punch fat cat

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the name is read backwards
a punch drives into something, so one word goes inside another

blocks.note: lard is pig fat
Edgar Allan Poe wrote horror tales

explanation.surface: A horror author is about to thump a rich, greedy businessman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat cat' reads as a wealthy executive, but fat is LARD and cat alone defines. POE reversed is EOP, which goes into LARD.
explanation.definitionFit: A leopard is a large spotted wild cat of Africa and Asia, so one member of the cat family.

clue.text: Entourage held back by vice unit erroneously

indicators.note: the letters are held within the words that follow
going back means read from right to left

blocks.note: a run of letters across the end of vice, all of unit and the start of erroneously

explanation.surface: A celebrity's hangers-on are detained by a police vice squad by mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of attendants and followers who accompany an important person.

clue.text: Claim Queen won't appear with Chrissie Hynde?

indicators.note: something that will not appear is absent, so it is taken out

blocks.note: Chrissie Hynde fronts the band the Pretenders, so one with her is a Pretender
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A queen pulling out of a gig alongside a rock singer.
explanation.walkthrough: Chrissie Hynde is lead singer of the rock band the Pretenders, so a member with her is a PRETENDER; remove ER.
explanation.definitionFit: To pretend can mean to lay claim to something, as a pretender claims a throne.
